title: Digital Humanitarian Network and Green Technologies
html:
Recently, one of my colleagues outlined a great parallel between the Digital Humanitarian Network (DHNetwork) and green technologies. It is one of the more clever and simplest analogies that I have heard to date so I wanted to share it.

The DHNetwork and the efforts by the Volunteer & Technical Communities can largely be seen in a similar way as green technologies: initially questioned and disregarded by the traditional market, rather “un-scalable” in the early days of their existence  and require a lot of lobbying and education to the larger population  However, for those involved in the market and versed on the subject, it is understood the they will play a major role in the future.  They will not go away and things will only improve as they mature and the traditional market accepts them. I guess the big question is when will we reach the tipping point where digital humanitarians are understood to be an essential responder in every emergency?

I am proud to have been a co-founder of the DHNetwork with Dr. Patrick Meier and to work with the great members who really made it happen: DataKind, ESRI, Geeks-Without-Bounds, GISCorps, Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team, Humanity Road, MapAction, Statistics Without Borders, Standby Volunteer Task Force, Translators Without Borders and UNV’s Online Volunteering.  As we approach the end of our first year in existence, now comes the challenge to make such efforts grow, to become scalable for any size of emergency and to improve information management in humanitarian response all around.  Of course, these efforts will take time and resources, but I truly hope that we are on the right path to move it forward.

There are many digital humanitiarian related projects around the world these days and I hope that their continued momentum that will push us, as a collective group, over the tipping point very soon.

Andrej
teaser: A colleague's analogy comparing the Digital Humanitarian Network to green technologies, and the question of when digital humanitarians reach a tipping point.
